title: Found a path. The shortest one?
hook: A search that always goes deeper first will find the exit. Will it find the quick way?

knows: a map as places joined by links
backing up when a corridor is a dead end
doesNotKnow: depth-first search and its stack of places
that the first path depth-first search finds need not be the shortest

misconception: The first path an exploring algorithm finds is the shortest.
objective: The learner can trace depth-first search on S-A, S-G, A-G (alphabetical) to S, A, G and explain that going deeper first finds a path but not necessarily the one with fewest links.

claims.text: On S-A, S-G, A-G, depth-first search from S trying neighbours alphabetically returns S, A, G: 2 links, though S, G is 1.
claims.source: Demo.tsx dfsSteps(TRIANGLE): S -> A (A before G), A's unvisited neighbour G -> stop; stack S, A, G. shortest() (breadth-first) gives S, G. Builder also ran an independent recursive DFS in Node: [S, A, G].

claims.text: In the bigger maze depth-first search hits the dead end B, backs up, and returns S, A, C, D, G (4 links) where S, E, G (2 links) would do. B was a dead end.
claims.source: Demo.tsx dfsSteps(MAZE) and shortest(MAZE) on the edges listed in MAZE (S-A, S-E, A-B, A-C, C-D, D-G, E-G). The maze was designed by the builder to show a long find; it is an illustration, not a typical case. | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Hand trace of dfsSteps with sorted neighbours: S-A-B (dead end, back to A)-C-D-G, 4 links; BFS gives S-E-G, 2 links. Stage message adds 'B was a dead end.' on the maze.

claims.text: Depth-first search commits to one branch and only backs up at a dead end, keeping the current path on a stack.
claims.source: Demo.tsx dfsSteps (explicit stack: push on a new neighbour, pop when none is left). CLRS 3rd ed., 22.3 'Depth-first search'.

claims.text: Depth-first search always finds a path if one exists, but not necessarily the shortest.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 22.3 (DFS visits every vertex reachable from the source; no shortest-path guarantee) contrasted with 22.2 (BFS computes shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs).

claims.text: To find the path with the fewest links, search breadth-first (every place one link away, then two, and so on).
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 22.2, Theorem 22.5 (breadth-first search computes shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs). | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): CLRS 3e 22.2, Theorem 22.5 (4e: 20.2, Theorem 20.5): BFS computes shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs.

recall.question: A robot explores a building depth-first and reports the first route it found to the exit. What can you say about that route?
options: It is a real route, but may be far from the shortest
It may not reach the exit
recall.why: Depth-first search follows one branch until it dead-ends, so it finds a route if one exists, but it commits to whichever branch it tried first, not the shortest.
